title: Farm to Table
description: Ten stories and reports about how food reaches our plates: a first season on a vegetable farm, a chef who buys only nearby, a tomato's journey, bees, an apple farm in winter, a farmers' market, a small cheese farm, a food bank, a market cooking contest and a bicycle delivery business.
topic: Farming, food and the people who bring it to the table

lessons.title: A First Season on the Farm
lessons.summary: A woman inherits her grandmother's vegetable farm and learns, season by season, to work it.
lessons.text:
When my grandmother died three years ago, she left me her farm: twelve acres of good soil, a red barn, a dozen hens and a notebook full of advice. At the time, I was working in an office in the city, and my friends assumed I would sell the land. Instead, I decided to treat the inheritance as an invitation. I gave up my apartment, moved into the farmhouse and became, at thirty-four, a complete beginner.

Being a beginner is humbling. In my first spring, I made almost every mistake that my grandmother's notebook warned against. I planted too early, while the ground was still cold and damp, and half of the seeds rotted before they could grow. The damp weather also brought the snails. They came out every evening at twilight and ate my young plants down to the roots. My grandmother had written, in her firm hand, "Snails are thugs. Be tougher than they are." At first I laughed at the word, but after a week of losing my salad greens to those slow little thugs, I understood her completely.

Her solution, as usual, was simple. She used to let the hens out in the late afternoon to eat every snail they could find. I did the same, and my hens turned out to be the best workers on the farm. Within a month, the snails had become rare.

The next problem came from the air. Small white butterflies laid eggs on my greens, and soon worms were eating holes in every leaf. This time, the notebook told me to cover the beds with fine mesh. I bought a roll of mesh, stretched it over bent wires and pinned it to the ground. The mesh let in the sun and the rain but kept the butterflies out, and by July my plants were whole and healthy.

Summer went by in a blur. I got up at five, worked until twilight and fell asleep over my dinner. Broadly speaking, the farm had two jobs that never ended: weeding and watering. Still, there were moments of pure pleasure. Nothing I had eaten in the city could compare with a crisp green leaf picked in the cool of the morning, or a carrot so crisp that it snapped like a stick.

By the end of October, I had sold vegetables at the local market every Saturday for four months. I had not made much money, but I had not lost any either, which, for a beginner, felt like a victory. One evening, I sat at the kitchen table with my grandmother's notebook and added a page of my own. "Broadly," I wrote, "the farm teaches patience. The hens teach the rest."

Questions:
How did the writer come to own a farm?
She received it as an inheritance from her grandmother.
Why did half of her seeds rot in the first spring?
She planted them too early, while the ground was still cold and damp.
Why did her grandmother call snails thugs?
Because they came out at twilight and ate the young plants.
How did the writer protect her greens from the butterflies?
She covered the beds with fine mesh, which let in the sun and the rain but kept the butterflies out.
What, broadly speaking, were the two jobs on the farm that never ended?
They were weeding and watering.

lessons.title: The Chef Who Counts the Miles
lessons.summary: A profile of a chef who buys all his food from farms within forty miles of his restaurant.
lessons.text:
Theo Grant does not have a list of suppliers; he has a map. On the wall of his small kitchen hangs a map of the county, and on it are fourteen pins, one for every farm that sells him food. None of the pins is more than forty miles from the restaurant.

Grant opened his restaurant, Field, six years ago, and it has since garnered a remarkable amount of praise. Last year it garnered a national award, and food enthusiasts now travel from other states to eat there. Yet his aspiration, he says, was never to be famous. His aspiration was to cook the way his mother did, with whatever the garden gave her that week.

That idea shapes everything on his menu. In most restaurants, the meat is the star and the vegetables play supporting roles. At Field, it is the other way around. "The vegetable is the protagonist," Grant explains. "The meat, if there is any, is a minor character." A typical dish might be a whole roasted carrot served with a spicy sauce made from peppers grown three miles away. The sauce is spicy enough to wake you up, but never so spicy that you lose the taste of the carrot.

When Grant does cook meat, nothing is wasted. He buys whole pigs from a family farm and uses every part. The fatty pieces that other kitchens throw away go into a slow process called rendering: the fat is heated gently for hours until it melts and separates from the meat. The rendering produces a clear, pure fat in which Grant fries his potatoes. Fatty cuts that a supermarket could hardly sell become, in his hands, the base of half the menu.

Critics and food enthusiasts have described a meal at Field as a symphony, and the comparison is a fair one. Each course is like a movement in a symphony, with its own mood, yet all of them belong to one piece. In June, the symphony is green and light; in November, it is brown, deep and warm.

Not everyone agrees with him. Some chefs argue that refusing lemons from abroad makes his work harder for no reason. Grant does not claim that food from far away is inferior. He simply believes that a tomato picked yesterday will beat one picked two weeks ago, and that a seasonal menu is not inferior just because it leaves certain things out.

He knows that he sometimes sounds like a preacher, and he laughs about it. "I try not to preach," he says. "A preacher tells you what to believe. I would rather feed you and let you decide for yourself."

Questions:
Why does Theo Grant have a map on his kitchen wall?
It shows the fourteen farms that sell him food, and none of them is more than forty miles away.
What was Grant's aspiration as a cook?
His aspiration was to cook the way his mother did, with whatever the garden gave her that week.
What does Grant mean when he calls the vegetable the protagonist?
He means that the vegetable is the main character, and the meat plays only a small role.
What is rendering?
It is a slow process in which fatty pieces of meat are heated gently until the fat melts and separates.
Why does Grant not want to be a preacher?
Because a preacher tells people what to believe, and he would rather let them decide.

lessons.title: The Long Road of a Tomato
lessons.summary: How a winter tomato travels from a southern greenhouse to a supermarket in the north.
lessons.text:
Pick up a tomato in a supermarket in January, and you are holding the end of a long journey. Globally, the tomato is one of the most widely grown vegetables, and globally it is also one of the most widely traded. In winter, the tomatoes in northern stores have often traveled more than a thousand miles.

The tomato begins in a greenhouse in the south, where the winter sun is still strong. It is picked while it is green and hard, because a ripe tomato is too soft to survive the trip. On this journey, picking must precede ripening; if the order were reversed, most of the fruit would arrive as sauce. Workers place each tomato gently in a shallow box and send the boxes to a packing house.

At the packing house, washing and sorting precede everything else. Each box is then checked for damage and compared with a benchmark, a standard for size and shape set by the buyers. Tomatoes that meet the benchmark go to supermarkets. Those that fall short of it are sent to factories that make soup.

Next comes the ripening room. Tomatoes, like bananas and apples, naturally emit a gas that tells the fruit to ripen. In a ripening room, managers add a little more of the same gas, so that the tomatoes turn red in a few days instead of two weeks. The room simply repeats, a little louder, a signal that the fruit would emit on its own.

A journey of two or three days is hard on soft fruit. Every bump in the road sends a vibration through the boxes, and hours of steady vibration can bruise a tomato from the inside. For this reason, the boxes are packed tightly so that the fruit cannot roll. The trucks are cooled, but not too much: below about 50 degrees, a tomato loses its flavor, and that loss cannot be undone.

Water matters as well, because a tomato that loses too much of it becomes soft. Careful packing helps with water retention, and good retention is one of the qualities that scientists look for when they develop new types of tomato.

At the distribution center, each store receives its allocation, which is based on what it sold the week before. A busy store in the city might receive an allocation of ninety boxes, a small store in a village only ten.

Finally, in the store itself, the staff refresh the display several times a day, removing damaged fruit and adding fresh boxes. The purpose of each refresh is to make the pile look as if it had just come from a field. Roughly ninety percent of the tomatoes that left the greenhouse reach that pile. When you choose one, you are choosing the winner of a remarkably long race.

Questions:
Why are winter tomatoes picked while they are still green?
Because a ripe tomato is too soft to survive the long trip.
What happens to tomatoes that fall short of the benchmark?
They are sent to factories that make soup.
What happens in the ripening room?
Managers add more of the gas that tomatoes emit naturally, so they turn red in a few days.
Why are the boxes packed tightly in the trucks?
Because the vibration from the road can bruise the fruit if it rolls.
How does a store's allocation of tomatoes depend on its sales?
Each store receives an allocation based on what it sold the week before.

lessons.title: The Bees and the Cherry Trees
lessons.summary: A woman who keeps bees explains how her colonies help the fruit farms in her valley.
lessons.text:
One cold morning in April, Ines Duarte loads forty wooden boxes onto a truck. Each box holds a colony of about twenty thousand bees. For the next three weeks, the bees will live among the cherry trees of a farm in the valley below, and the farmer will pay Duarte for every box.

The arrangement rests on a partnership that is millions of years old. Flowers cannot move, yet to make fruit, they need a fine yellow dust from other flowers of their kind. Bees visit flowers for the sweet liquid inside them, and as they fly from one to the next, they carry that dust with them. "It is an evolutionary bargain," Duarte says. "Flowers became brighter and sweeter to attract bees, and bees became better at finding flowers. Neither side planned it. Evolutionary pressure did the planning."

A single bee achieves very little. Collectively, however, a colony is remarkable. Its members visit millions of flowers in a season and collectively make decisions that no single bee could make. "Nobody is in charge," Duarte says. "They decide collectively, like a town meeting with twenty thousand voters."

The colony's home is also a fortress. Guard bees stand at the entrance and check every bee that arrives, and the colony seals every crack with a sticky substance that it collects from trees. "Inside, the fortress is warm, dark and clean," Duarte explains. "A wasp that tries to get in rarely gets out again."

In the cold months, the bees are confined to the box, sometimes for weeks at a time. While they are confined, they cluster together to stay warm, living on the honey they stored in summer, so Duarte never takes all of it. Honey extraction happens only once a year, in August. She cuts the wax lids off the frames and spins them in a machine, so that the honey flies out. The extraction leaves her kitchen and her hair completely sticky, but each colony keeps enough honey to survive until spring.

Her greatest worry is food. In a valley planted with only one or two crops, bees can suffer from a deficiency of variety, much as a person would if he ate nothing but apples. To prevent such a deficiency, Duarte intentionally plants wild flowers around her yard. Several farmers now intentionally leave strips of wild flowers between their trees.

Those strips enrich the soil, shelter birds and, according to Duarte, enrich the farmers' lives as well. "One of them told me that he now goes wandering through the flowers before work, just to listen to the bees," she says. "Wandering is not wasted time. The bees spend their whole day wandering, and look how much they get done."

Questions:
Why does the farmer pay Ines Duarte in April?
Because her bees live among his cherry trees for three weeks and help them make fruit.
What does Duarte mean by an evolutionary bargain?
She means that flowers and bees developed together because each side needed the other.
Why does she compare the colony to a fortress?
Because guard bees check every bee at the entrance, and the bees seal every crack with a sticky substance.
What do the bees live on while they are confined to the box in winter?
They live on the honey they stored in summer.
How does Duarte try to prevent a deficiency in the bees' diet?
She intentionally plants wild flowers, and several farmers leave strips of them between their trees.

lessons.title: The Apple Trees in Winter
lessons.summary: An old apple grower spends the winter cutting, checking and reading, to prepare his trees for spring.
lessons.text:
In January, Walter Hayes's apple farm looks like a place where nothing is happening. The trees stand bare in their long rows, and the air smells of cold earth. Yet Walter, who has grown apples here for forty years, insists that winter is when next year's harvest is decided.

Every morning after breakfast, he wraps a thick wool scarf twice around his neck and walks out with a pair of sharp cutters. His wife knitted it for him twenty winters ago, and he refuses to wear another. His work in these months is cutting back the trees. He removes the woody growth of last summer: long, straight shoots that point at the sky and steal light from the fruit below. Left alone, a tree becomes a mess of woody branches with small, poor apples.

Walter also checks the alignment of his younger trees. Each tree is tied to a post, and the posts must stand in a perfectly straight line. If the alignment is off by even a few inches, the machine that sprays the trees in summer cannot pass between the rows. After every storm, he walks the rows with a long string, correcting the alignment one post at a time.

The cold itself does not worry him. Apple trees defy the winter. Their buds are wrapped in tight scales, and their wood can survive temperatures far below freezing. "They don't fight the cold," he says. "They sleep through it. That is how they defy it."

When the light fades, Walter retreats to the cozy kitchen, where a wood stove burns all day. In that cozy room, he reads about soil. His valley has an unusual geological history. Thousands of years ago, a glacier pushed through it and left behind a thick layer of crushed limestone. That geological accident is the reason his apples are so good: limestone is rich in calcium, and apples need calcium to stay firm. A tree with inadequate calcium produces fruit with small brown spots under the skin, which spoil in storage. Even on his land, the supply is sometimes inadequate, so each winter he spreads a little lime on the poorest rows.

On the kitchen shelf sits a heavy atlas of apples, with paintings of more than a thousand varieties. On winter evenings, Walter opens the atlas and looks for old varieties that most farmers have overlooked. Many of them taste wonderful but look plain, which is why the supermarkets overlooked them long ago. This spring, he plans to plant six of them.

By March, the cutting is finished, and the trees stand neat and open. Walter hangs his scarf by the stove, satisfied. The farm looks as still as ever, but he knows that it is ready.

Questions:
What does Walter remove from his trees in winter?
He removes last summer's woody growth, the long shoots that steal light from the fruit.
Why must the alignment of the posts be perfect?
Because otherwise the machine that sprays the trees in summer cannot pass between the rows.
How do apple trees defy the winter?
Their buds are wrapped in tight scales, and they sleep through the cold.
Why is the valley's geological history good for his apples?
A glacier left a layer of limestone, which is rich in the calcium that apples need to stay firm.
What does Walter look for in his atlas of apples?
He looks for old varieties that most farmers and the supermarkets have overlooked.

lessons.title: Running the Market
lessons.summary: The manager of a town's farmers' market describes a website, a newsletter, a fee and a new building.
lessons.text:
Every Saturday from May to October, the old square in the center of our town fills with sixty white tents, and I make sure each one is in the right place. I have managed the farmers' market for seven years. People imagine that my job is mostly tasting peaches. In reality, it is mostly paperwork, phone calls and, lately, computers.

Three years ago, the market had no website and no list of customers. All we had was a paper newsletter, which I printed every month and left in a box by the fountain. The pigeons that live on the square seemed to enjoy it more than the people did. I often found the newsletter scattered across the stones, with a pigeon standing proudly on top of it.

So I asked for help from an old classmate, Daniel, whom I had known since we were eleven. Daniel is a programmer, and he agreed to build us a simple website on weekends. He wrote it in Python, a programming language that he says is easy to read, even for a beginner.

The new site let customers sign up for an email newsletter. Each person chose a username and a password, and every Thursday they received a list of what the farmers would bring. Within a month, we had eight hundred readers. Some people signed up twice, creating a duplicate account and receiving two copies. Daniel wrote a few lines of Python that searched for duplicate addresses and removed them. One woman forgot her username four times in a single week. In the end, I wrote it on a card for her.

The next year, the town decided that every seller at the market needed a permit and had to pay a fee. For a large farm, the fee was nothing; for a grandmother selling twelve jars of jam, it was more than she earned in a day. I wrote letters, attended meetings and finally persuaded the town to grant an exemption for the smallest sellers. The exemption covers anyone who earns less than a certain amount each season. It was the proudest moment of my working life.

Last year, a tall condominium with sixty apartments went up on the north side of the square. Some farmers feared that the people in the condominium would complain about the noise and the early trucks. The opposite happened. They are now among our most loyal customers, and several of them come down every Saturday in their slippers.

What I have learned is that a market is not just a place to buy food. It is a place of enjoyment: children eating the first strawberries and old friends meeting by the fountain. My job is to protect that enjoyment, even when it means filling out forms and chasing pigeons away from the newsletter box.

Questions:
What happened to the paper newsletter that the writer left by the fountain?
It was often scattered across the stones, with a pigeon standing on it.
Who built the market's website, and how?
Her old classmate Daniel, a programmer, built it on weekends and wrote it in Python.
Why did some customers receive two copies of the newsletter?
Because they had signed up twice and created a duplicate account.
What exemption did the writer win from the town?
She persuaded the town not to charge the permit fee to the smallest sellers.
How did the people in the new condominium react to the market?
They became some of the market's most loyal customers.

lessons.title: Cheese, Slowly
lessons.summary: A former chemistry lecturer explains, step by step, how her small farm turns milk into cheese.
lessons.text:
Helen Kowalski spent fifteen years as a chemistry lecturer at a state university before she bought a small dairy farm with thirty cows. She still explains cheese the way a lecturer explains a chemical reaction, one step at a time. "Cheese," she tells visitors, "is milk with most of the water taken out. Everything else is detail."

The detail begins with what the cows eat. In winter, they eat hay made mostly from timothy, a tall grass that grows well in the cool, wet hills around the farm. Timothy is soft and sweet, and Kowalski believes that cows fed on timothy give milk with a fuller flavor.

Each morning, the warm milk flows into a large steel tank. Kowalski heats it gently and adds two things. The first is a culture of friendly bacteria, which slowly turns some of the milk's sugar into acid. The second is a substance that makes the milk set like a soft jelly. The amounts are tiny: for milk that will become a hundred pounds of cheese, she uses only a few grams of that substance. A few grams too many, and the cheese turns bitter; too few, and it never sets.

How does she know when the milk is ready? She measures the acid, which serves as a proxy for what is happening in the tank. She cannot see the bacteria at work, but the level of acid is a reliable proxy for their progress. When it reaches the right number, she cuts the soft milk into small cubes, and a pale liquid begins to separate from the solid pieces. The pieces are salted and pressed into round forms.

Cheese was probably an accidental discovery. Thousands of years ago, people carried milk in bags made from the stomachs of young animals. Those stomachs contain the same substance she adds today, so the milk inside turned into cheese on its own. "It was an accidental invention," she says, "but somebody was clever enough to repeat it on purpose."

Then comes the waiting. Beneath the house, a long, cool hallway runs underground, lined on both sides with shelves of round cheeses. Every week, Kowalski walks the hallway and turns each cheese by hand. The hallway smells of earth, salt and something like roasted nuts.

There is one kind of milk that she never uses. For a few days after a cow gives birth, her milk is thick, yellow and full of antibodies, which protect the newborn calf from disease until its own body can make antibodies. "That milk belongs to the calf," Kowalski says.

After a year, her best cheeses go to restaurants and to the farmers' market. She still thinks of herself as a lecturer. The only difference, she says, is that her lessons now come in slices.

Questions:
What did Helen Kowalski do before she became a farmer?
She was a chemistry lecturer at a state university for fifteen years.
What do her cows eat in winter?
They eat hay made mostly from timothy, a tall grass.
Why does she measure the acid in the milk?
Because the level of acid is a proxy for the work of the bacteria, which she cannot see.
Why does she call cheese an accidental invention?
Because milk carried in bags made from animal stomachs turned into cheese by accident.
Why does she never use the milk a cow gives just after birth?
Because it is full of antibodies that protect the newborn calf.

lessons.title: Rescuing Good Food
lessons.summary: A woman who runs a food bank collects food that stores would throw away and gives it to families in need.
lessons.text:
Every evening, in a city of half a million people, a remarkable amount of good food is thrown away. Bakeries throw out bread that did not sell, and supermarkets remove yogurt that is close to its date. Experts often measure such waste per capita, that is, per person, and the numbers are striking. In this country, the waste per capita comes to roughly a pound of food every day.

Grace Okafor has spent ten years trying to change that number. She runs a food bank from an old warehouse on the east side of the city, with two vans that keep food cold. Its mission is simple: collect food that stores would throw away and deliver it the same day to people who need it.

Most of the food she collects is perfectly good. The problem, Grace explains, lies in the dates printed on packages. "Those dates deceive people," she says. "A 'best before' date is about quality, not safety. Shoppers think a yogurt is worthless the day after that date, when in fact it is fine for a week or more." As a result, tons of food that is far from worthless end up in the trash.

Her volunteers include students and retired teachers. Her most reliable driver is a retired firefighter named Frank, who spent thirty years with the city's fire department. "Firefighters know how to work fast and stay calm," Grace says. "Frank treats every pickup like an emergency, in the best possible way."

Frank's van is old, and last winter, on the coldest morning of the year, it refused to start. He turned the key in the ignition again and again, but the engine only coughed. A mechanic later found that the ignition had worn out. That same week, a breaker in the warehouse's electrical panel failed, and the cold room began to warm up. Volunteers moved a ton of milk and cheese into the vans before it could spoil, and an electrician replaced the breaker by noon.

The following spring, two large factories in the city closed, and demand at the food bank rose to an unprecedented level. In April, the food bank served more families than in any month of its history. In May, it broke that unprecedented record again. What carried Grace through those months was the willingness of ordinary people to help. Store managers called to offer more food, and dozens of new volunteers appeared. That willingness, she says, is the food bank's real engine.

Some families, especially recent immigrants, are afraid to ask for help at all. A few worry that giving their names could get them deported. Grace understands the fear and answers it clearly: the food bank never asks for papers, never shares its lists and has nothing to do with the officials who deport people. "We ask one question," she says. "Are you hungry?"

Questions:
How much food does the waste per capita come to in this country?
It comes to roughly a pound of food per person every day.
How do the dates on packages deceive shoppers?
Shoppers think a product is worthless after its "best before" date, although the date is about quality, not safety.
Who is Grace's most reliable driver?
He is Frank, a retired firefighter.
What went wrong at the food bank last winter?
The ignition in Frank's van wore out, and a breaker failed in the warehouse.
What carried Grace through the months of unprecedented demand?
The willingness of ordinary people to help carried her through.

lessons.title: The Market Cooking Contest
lessons.summary: A nurse enters a cooking contest at the farmers' market with her grandfather's recipe and reaches the final.
lessons.text:
Each September, the farmers' market holds a cooking contest, and this year Lucy Park decided to enter. Lucy was not a professional cook but a nurse at the county hospital, and she cooked mostly from recipes she had learned from her grandpa, who had run a small restaurant for forty years.

Each contender had to cook two dishes using only food sold at the market that morning. The first dish was a recipe of the cook's own choice. The second was a freestyle round: each contender received a basket of vegetables chosen by the judges and had one hour to create whatever she or he liked. The freestyle round was what worried Lucy most. She was used to following her grandpa's recipes, not inventing her own.

Twenty-four people entered, and after the first round, the judges chose six finalists. To her delight, Lucy was one of them. Her dish was her grandpa's chicken stew with fresh corn, and one judge said it tasted like a Sunday afternoon. When the market's spokesman read out the names of the finalists through a microphone, Lucy felt her stomach turn a somersault. She had never imagined that she would get this far.

The final took place on a small stage. Because the stage stood in the center of the market, the cooks had a captive audience: nobody could reach the fruit stands without walking past them, and soon hundreds of shoppers had stopped to watch. The spokesman walked from table to table with his microphone, asking each finalist what she or he was making. That captive audience made Lucy more nervous than any emergency at the hospital.

Lucy's basket held carrots, beets, small hot peppers and goat cheese. For a moment, her mind went blank. Then she remembered something her grandpa used to say: "When you don't know what to do, roast it." She roasted the carrots and beets until their edges were dark and sweet, broke the cheese over them and made a sauce from the peppers, honey and lemon. Her stomach did another somersault as she set the plate in front of the judges.

The other contenders were strong. One was a young chef from a downtown restaurant; another was a retired baker who had won the contest twice before. When the judges had finished tasting, the spokesman stepped up to the microphone and announced the results. The baker won for the third time, and Lucy came second. She was the first to congratulate the winner.

That night, Lucy called her grandpa, who was now ninety and lived with her aunt. She told him everything. He listened, then asked only one question: "Did you roast it?" When she said yes, he laughed and told her that, whatever the judges thought, she had won.

Questions:
Where did Lucy learn most of her recipes?
She learned them from her grandpa.
What was the freestyle round?
Each contender received a basket of vegetables chosen by the judges and had one hour to create a dish.
How did Lucy feel when the spokesman read her name as a finalist?
She felt her stomach turn a somersault, because she had never imagined getting that far.
Why did the cooks have a captive audience?
Because the stage was in the center of the market, where every shopper had to walk past it.
What did Lucy cook in the freestyle round?
She roasted the carrots and beets, added the goat cheese and made a sauce from the peppers.

lessons.title: Pedaling the Harvest
lessons.summary: A former college football player recovers from an injury and starts a business delivering farm food by bicycle.
lessons.text:
Marcus Bell used to make his living with his legs, and in a way he still does. For four years, he played cornerback for his college football team. A cornerback must stay close to the fastest player on the other team and stop him from catching the ball. Marcus was quick and brave, and many people thought he might become a professional. Then, in his last season, he badly injured his knee.

The months of rehab that followed were the hardest of his life. Three times a week, he went to a rehab center, where a therapist made him ride an exercise bike. During each visit, Marcus had to pedal for forty minutes. At first, he could barely pedal for five. Slowly, the minutes grew, and so did his strength.

By the end of his rehab, his knee was healthy again, but not strong enough for a professional cornerback. Marcus was disappointed, yet he had discovered that he loved riding. When he finished college, he bought a cargo bike, a heavy bicycle with a large box in front, and started a small business delivering food from local farms to homes across the city.

Today, his company has six riders and eleven bikes. Every morning, they pedal out to the farms on the edge of town, load boxes of vegetables, eggs and cheese, and pedal back to deliver them before noon. On Fridays, Marcus also stops at a small fishery by the harbor, a family business that sells only the fish caught that morning by its own boats. The fishery packs the fish in ice, and Marcus brings it to restaurants within an hour.

Marcus has seen plenty of reckless drivers: people who turn without looking or read their phones at red lights. He trains each new rider to assume that any driver might be reckless. "Ride as if nobody can see you," he tells them. "Then nothing a driver does will catch you off guard."

Finding an insurer was harder than he had expected. The first three companies he called had never covered a cargo bike business. The fourth insurer agreed, after Marcus showed its staff his training program and his record: in three years, not one serious accident.

One of his favorite customers is Mrs. Alvarez, an older woman with diabetes who orders a box every week. She once told Marcus that eating more fresh vegetables had helped her doctor lower her daily dose of insulin. Marcus does not know much about insulin, but her box is always the first one he delivers on Tuesday mornings.

Sometimes, when he climbs a steep hill with sixty pounds of potatoes in front of him, Marcus thinks of the exercise bike in the rehab center. "Back then, I was pedaling to nowhere," he says. "Now I am pedaling somewhere that matters."

Questions:
What position did Marcus play on his college football team?
He played cornerback, which meant staying close to the fastest player on the other team.
What did Marcus have to do during his rehab?
He had to pedal an exercise bike for forty minutes at each visit.
What does Marcus pick up at the fishery on Fridays?
He picks up fish caught that morning and brings it to restaurants within an hour.
What does Marcus tell new riders about reckless drivers?
He tells them to ride as if nobody can see them.
Why did the fourth insurer agree to cover his business?
Because Marcus showed its staff his training program and his safety record.
